summary: Deep, wide catalog of concrete AI agent examples across founder ops domains, built for a hands-on workshop
logs: Collected 81 candidate agent ideas across 7 domains

survivors.name: Smart Lead Qualifier & Outreach Drafter (Runway-style)
survivors.trigger: New demo-request/signup row written to a database (e.g., Retool, Typeform, webform-to-Sheet) fires a webhook
survivors.tools_touched: Webhook -> Filter (free-email domain check) -> Clearbit (company enrichment: size, industry, location) -> ChatGPT (fit scoring against ICP rules) -> Gmail (drafts) / Slack (notify rep)
survivors.autonomous_action: Filters out consumer-domain signups, enriches the remaining leads with firmographic data, has the LLM classify Qualified/Unqualified against explicit criteria (revenue, headcount, industry), and for Qualified leads autonomously drafts a personalized, context-aware email as a Gmail draft (human sends) plus posts a Slack alert to the rep — all within seconds of signup, no human touches it until the draft is ready.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: Requires branching logic across three live systems (DB webhook, Clearbit API, Gmail API), a stateful decision (qualified vs not) that changes the downstream path, and enrichment data the LLM doesn't have in its context window — a single prompt has no live company data and can't itself call Clearbit, filter records, or create a Gmail draft.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: High — this is literally shipped as a Zapier template today; the same shape (webhook trigger, HTTP/Clearbit module, OpenAI module, router/filter, Gmail module) maps 1:1 onto Make.com scenario modules.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, unambiguously. Every slot in the pipeline names a specific, real tool and a specific action, not a category:
- Trigger is specific: "new demo-request/signup row written to a DB fires a webhook" — a named event, not "when a lead comes in."
- Tool chain is a named sequence: Webhook -> Filter -> Clearbit -> ChatGPT -> Gmail/Slack. Each has a concrete role (free-email domain check; firmographic enrichment; fit scoring against explicit ICP fields of revenue/headcount/industry; draft creation; rep notification).
- The autonomous action is scoped precisely: LLM classifies against explicit criteria, drafts land in Gmail as drafts (not sent), Slack alert fires in parallel — and a human-in-the-loop gate is explicitly named ("human sends"). That's a specific action boundary, not a vague "AI handles outreach."
- This clears the bar the S2 gap canon uses for concreteness far better than a vague "an agent that qualifies leads" pitch would.

FEASIBLE on Make.com in a workshop: Yes, with minor caveats worth flagging but not disqualifying.
- Webhook trigger: native Make.com module (Webhooks > Custom webhook), trivial to wire from Typeform/Retool/Sheet-append.
- Filter: native Make.com filter/router on webhook payload (email domain regex against a free-provider list) — no custom code needed, this is bread-and-butter Make.com.
- Clearbit: has a documented REST API; Make.com has no dedicated Clearbit app-connector I can confirm, but it's a simple bearer-token HTTP GET, so an HTTP module handles it in one step — well within workshop scope and consistent with how Make.com scenarios normally reach third-party APIs.
- OpenAI/ChatGPT: Make.com has a first-party OpenAI (ChatGPT) app module — one of its most common integrations, trivial to configure with a prompt template that takes enrichment fields as variables.
- Gmail "create draft" and Slack "post message": both are first-party Make.com app modules, among the most commonly demoed in Make.com tutorials.
- Runtime is "within seconds" — realistic for a webhook-triggered linear scenario with 5 modules; no async/long-polling problem.
- Only soft risk: Clearbit now sits under HubSpot/Breeze branding and free-tier signup friction could eat workshop time — but that's a provisioning/account-creation logistics issue, not a feasibility-of-wiring issue, and a workshop can substitute any enrichment API (People Data Labs, Apollo) or even a stubbed HTTP call with canned JSON without changing the scenario shape.
- The claimed prior art (Zapier template for Runway-style lead qual) is a reasonable existence proof of shape, though I did not independently verify the source_url resolves — that's a citation-grounding caveat on the idea's supporting evidence, not on the workflow's buildability, since the module-level feasibility stands on Make.com's own documented app library regardless of whether that specific blog post is accurate.

Net: this is a well-specified, buildable, appropriately-scoped-for-a-workshop idea. It should pass.

survivors.name: Sales Prospect Research & Outreach Brief Generator
survivors.trigger: Rep submits a name + company (form, Sheet row, or Slack command) for a target prospect
survivors.tools_touched: Apollo.io API (contact + LinkedIn URL lookup) -> Linkup API (reads/analyzes the public LinkedIn profile) -> OpenAI (synthesizes overview, pain points, value-prop alignment) -> output written to CRM field or Sheet/Doc
survivors.autonomous_action: Chains two external data lookups (contact data, then profile scraping/analysis) and has the LLM synthesize a three-part research brief — overview, likely pain points, and how the rep's offering maps to them — using the rep's own business context as a lens, then writes the consolidated brief into a CRM-ready record without the rep doing any manual lookup.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: The LLM alone has no access to the prospect's actual current employer, title, or LinkedIn content; it needs two sequential live API calls (Apollo then Linkup) whose outputs feed the prompt, plus a final write-back step — a single static prompt can't fetch or sequence that.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: High — Apollo and generic HTTP/scraping modules plus an OpenAI module are standard Make.com building blocks; this is a direct port of a published n8n workflow.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: trigger (form/Sheet/Slack with name+company), tools (Apollo.io API, Linkup API, OpenAI), and action (sequential lookup -> profile analysis -> 3-part LLM synthesis -> CRM/Sheet write-back) are all specifically named, not vague categories. Verified against the source n8n workflow (n8n.io/workflows/6492) via WebFetch — the trigger, node chain (Apollo enrich -> Linkup profile analysis -> consolidation -> CRM-ready output), and business-context-as-lens mechanic all match. One minor inaccuracy: in the source, Linkup itself does the synthesis and OpenAI is only an optional extension for email drafting, not the stated synthesis engine — but substituting an explicit OpenAI/LLM module for that synthesis step in the Make.com port is a trivial, workshop-appropriate simplification that doesn't affect feasibility.

FEASIBLE on Make.com: Apollo.io and Linkup have no native Make.com modules but both expose standard REST APIs callable via Make's generic HTTP module (a bog-standard pattern), OpenAI has a first-class native Make module, and Make's linear scenario model is exactly suited to chaining sequential API outputs into a prompt and then to a write-back module (Google Sheets/Docs/HubSpot/Airtable all natively supported). Realistic workshop build is ~4-5 modules. The one real cost is needing three separate API credentials (Apollo, Linkup, OpenAI) pre-provisioned to avoid burning live workshop time on signups — a logistics caveat, not an infeasibility. Also worth flagging as a caveat (not a build blocker): LinkedIn-profile-reading APIs like Linkup sit in a ToS/reliability gray zone for production use, though this doesn't block wiring up a workshop demo.

survivors.name: Meeting-Notes-to-CRM Autopilot (Fireflies/Gong-style)
survivors.trigger: A sales call ends (calendar event with a recording bot joins Zoom/Meet/Teams)
survivors.tools_touched: Fireflies or Gong (transcription + summarization) -> LLM (extracts action items, objections, next steps, deal-stage signals) -> CRM (HubSpot/Salesforce field/stage update) -> Slack (routes summary to deal owner/channel)
survivors.autonomous_action: Automatically records and transcribes the call, extracts structured fields (objections raised, commitments made, suggested next deal stage) via LLM reasoning over the transcript, writes those fields directly into the CRM deal record, and routes a summary to Slack — with zero manual note-taking or CRM data entry by the rep.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: Requires audio capture and transcription infrastructure, a retrieval step over a long transcript, structured extraction mapped to specific CRM schema fields, and a write-back action to a third system — a prompt has no transcript to read and no CRM API access on its own.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: High — Fireflies has a native Zapier/webhook + GraphQL API that Make.com can call directly; CRM and Slack modules are native Make.com connectors, making this one of the more turnkey builds.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, clearly. The trigger is specific (calendar event with a recording bot joining Zoom/Meet/Teams, firing Fireflies' "Transcription complete" webhook), not a vague "when a call happens." Tools are named precisely — Fireflies GraphQL API/webhook, not a generic "transcription tool" — with named CRM targets (HubSpot/Salesforce) and named output fields (objections raised, commitments made, suggested next deal stage). This is a fully specified pipeline, not a hand-wavy category.

FEASIBLE on Make.com: Verified via web search that all the load-bearing technical claims check out:
- Fireflies has a real webhook (x-hub-signature HMAC-verified) firing on "Transcription complete," and Make.com has a native Fireflies.ai app/connector plus generic HTTP/GraphQL module support (make.com/en/integrations/fireflies-ai).
- Fireflies' calendar auto-join into Zoom/Meet/Teams is a real, documented feature (guide.fireflies.ai), not invented.
- Make.com has long-standing native HubSpot and Salesforce connectors with deal/record update modules, and a native Slack message module — these are some of the most mature connectors on the platform.

One real gap the pitch glosses over, which keeps this from being a flawless plan but doesn't sink feasibility: the trigger ("a sales call ends") can't be manually fired in a workshop the way a form submission or button-click can — you'd need either a pre-recorded/pre-transcribed sample call in Fireflies, or to simulate by hand-feeding a saved transcript into the LLM→CRM→Slack half of the scenario. This is a standard, easy workaround (skip live trigger, demo from a canned transcript) but the write-up doesn't flag it, presenting the live-call trigger as if it's workshop-demoable as-is. Also assumes attendees already have HubSpot/Salesforce/Slack provisioned with admin API access, which is a fair "bring your own stack" assumption for this workshop genre but a real prerequisite. Neither issue changes the verdict — the idea is concrete and the connectors are real and native — but the trigger-simulation workaround should be called out explicitly when presented to founders so no one is surprised mid-build.

survivors.name: Deal Pipeline Watcher / Stagnation Flagger
survivors.trigger: Daily scheduled scan of all open CRM deals
survivors.tools_touched: CRM API (HubSpot/Salesforce/Pipedrive) -> LLM (reasons over last-activity-date, stage, deal value to classify risk) -> Slack/email digest to rep or founder
survivors.autonomous_action: Runs every day without being asked, cross-references each open deal's last-touch date and stage against expected velocity, autonomously classifies which deals have gone quiet or are unusually hot, and pushes a prioritized daily digest so the founder/rep only spends time on deals the system flagged — replacing a manual weekly pipeline review.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: The judgment ('this deal is stagnating') depends on live, per-deal state compared against a moving baseline (time elapsed, activity count) that must be recomputed daily by querying the CRM — there is no fixed prompt input since the entire pipeline changes every day.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: High — a Make.com scenario with a daily scheduler trigger, a CRM 'search records' module, an iterator, an OpenAI module for the risk classification, and a digest email/Slack module is a standard, well-supported pattern.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, on all three required dimensions.
- Trigger: specific and unambiguous — "daily scheduled scan of all open CRM deals" maps directly to a Make.com scheduler module (interval trigger) feeding a CRM search/list module. Not vague ("periodically check things").
- Tools: named concretely — HubSpot/Salesforce/Pipedrive as the CRM source (all three have first-party or well-supported Make.com modules), an LLM step (OpenAI module) for classification, and Slack/email for output. Each hop in the chain is a real, nameable Make.com module, not a hand-waved "integrate with CRM."
- Action: specific and falsifiable — cross-reference last-activity-date + stage + deal value against an expected-velocity baseline, classify into a risk bucket (stagnating vs hot), and push a prioritized digest. This is a well-defined transformation, not "analyze the pipeline" left undefined.

FEASIBLE for a no-code Make.com workshop build, even simplified:
- Scheduler module: native, trivial.
- CRM search/list module: HubSpot, Pipedrive, and Salesforce all have mature Make.com apps with a "Search/List Deals" or equivalent action returning stage, last-activity timestamp, and amount — exactly the three fields the logic needs. This is standard, heavily-documented Make.com territory (the cited make.com/en/solutions/automate-sales page is a legitimate, on-topic source, not a stretch citation).
- Iterator: native Make.com module, standard pattern for looping over an array of deals returned by a search.
- OpenAI module for classification: native Make.com OpenAI app, "Create a Completion/Chat Completion" action — feeding it per-deal fields (days since last touch, stage, value) and asking for a risk label + one-line reason is a bounded, well-scoped prompt. This is squarely the kind of judgment call an LLM step is good at and a fixed rule engine would need constant retuning for (variable expected velocity per stage/deal size).
- Aggregator + digest: Make.com's "Array Aggregator" or simple text aggregation into a Slack message/email module — standard, no custom code needed.
- Realistic simplification for a workshop: cap it at one CRM (e.g., Pipedrive test account, easiest sandbox to spin up), a handful of seeded fake deals, and skip nuanced velocity baselining in favor of a simple "days since last activity > threshold" rule combined with the LLM step for the qualitative "hot deal" judgment and prioritized write-up. That's buildable live in a 60-90 minute session.

Why this passes the "agentic, not prompt" bar: the reasoning target (which deals are stagnating) depends on live, per-deal state pulled fresh from the CRM every run, not a static prompt — this justifies the tool-calling/data-fetch architecture rather than a single canned prompt, consistent with the stated rationale.

Minor caveats (not disqualifying): "expected velocity per stage" implies a benchmark table that isn't specified — in a workshop this would need to be simplified to a flat day-threshold or a small hardcoded per-stage table, which the idea's own feasibility note implicitly allows for. Also, Salesforce's API/module setup has more friction (OAuth app approval, sandbox access) than HubSpot/Pipedrive for a live workshop, so the facilitator should steer toward Pipedrive or HubSpot as the demo CRM rather than presenting all three as equally easy — but this is an implementation detail, not a concreteness/feasibility failure of the idea itself.

survivors.name: Competitor & Market Intelligence Digest for Sales Talking Points
survivors.trigger: Scheduled crawl (daily/weekly) of competitor websites, pricing pages, and news sources
survivors.tools_touched: Firecrawl or Bright Data (scrapes competitor sites/pricing pages) -> diff/change-detection logic -> LLM (analyzes what changed and drafts sales talking points) -> Slack digest to sales team, optionally triggers a sub-workflow tied to specific open deals
survivors.autonomous_action: Autonomously re-scrapes competitor pages on a schedule, detects meaningful changes (price drop, new feature, news mention) versus the last snapshot, has the LLM interpret the significance and draft rep-ready talking points, and delivers a formatted digest — and can trigger a targeted alert to reps with open deals against that specific competitor.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: Needs persistent state (yesterday's page snapshot vs today's) to detect a *change*, live scraping the model has no access to, and conditional downstream branching to specific deal owners — a prompt has no memory of prior page state and can't crawl the web itself.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: High — Make.com's HTTP/Firecrawl modules plus a data-store module (to hold the last snapshot for diffing) plus OpenAI and Slack modules cover this end to end; this exact shape exists as a published n8n template.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE — yes, on every axis:
- Trigger is specific: scheduled crawl (daily/weekly) of named target types (competitor websites, pricing pages, news sources), not "monitor the market."
- Tools are named products, not categories: Firecrawl/Bright Data for scraping, a diff/change-detection step, an LLM step, Slack for delivery, plus an optional sub-workflow branch to deal owners. Each maps to a real Make.com module class (HTTP/Firecrawl app module, Data Store module for snapshot persistence, OpenAI module, Slack module, Router/Filter for branching).
- Action is a well-defined pipeline, not a vague "keep sales informed": scrape -> diff against last snapshot -> LLM interprets significance -> drafts rep-ready talking points -> Slack digest -> optional targeted alert to reps with open deals against that competitor. That's five concrete stages with clear inputs/outputs at each hop.
- The "why agentic not prompt" justification is correctly reasoned, not hand-wavy: it correctly identifies the two things a bare prompt genuinely cannot do — hold persistent state across runs (yesterday's snapshot) and reach out to fetch live web content — and ties the conditional branching (deal-owner routing) to needing workflow logic, not just a smarter prompt. This is a legitimate agentic justification, unlike degenerate "summarize this text" cases dressed up as agents.

FEASIBLE on Make.com in a workshop setting — with caveats worth flagging but not disqualifying:
- Scraping: Firecrawl has a native Make.com app/module; Bright Data can be wired via HTTP module. Either works in a 2-3 hour workshop slot for 1-2 competitor URLs.
- Diff/state: Make.com's Data Store module is real and commonly used exactly for this pattern (store last snapshot, compare on next run) — this is not an invented feature.
- LLM step: standard OpenAI module, trivial.
- Delivery: Slack module, trivial.
- Precedent: the cited n8n template (n8n.io/workflows/3101) demonstrates this exact shape has been built and published before, which is reasonable corroborating evidence the pipeline shape is sound — though it's an n8n template, not a Make.com one, so "this exact shape exists as a published n8n template" is true as stated but shouldn't be overstated as proof of Make.com feasibility; it's evidence of the *logical* pipeline's soundness, and Make.com has equivalent primitives (HTTP/Firecrawl, Data Store, OpenAI, Slack, Router) to reproduce it.

Workshop-simplification risks (real, but scope down rather than kill the idea):
- Full diffing (structured price/feature diff, not just raw HTML diff) usually needs a semantic diff step or an LLM-as-differ rather than naive text diff, since pricing pages have lots of noise (session tokens, timestamps, ads) that would trigger false positives on a raw HTML compare. In a workshop, this is best simplified to "LLM reads old snapshot + new snapshot text and decides if there's a meaningful change" rather than a byte-level diff — the proposal already gestures at this ("LLM analyzes what changed"), so it's compatible, just needs the facilitator to steer learners away from naive HTML diffing.
- Scraping is legally/ToS gray for some competitor sites (bot-blocking, robots.txt) — a workshop caveat, not a design flaw.
- The "sub-workflow tied to specific open deals" branch implies a CRM data source (deal owner mapping) that isn't named in tools_touched — this is the one soft spot: it's plausible (a Google Sheet or lightweight CRM lookup) but the proposal doesn't specify where "open deals against that competitor" data lives. This should be simplified/flagged in the workshop as "maintain a simple Sheet mapping competitor -> deal owner" rather than assuming a full CRM integration — but it doesn't break the core digest workflow, which stands alone even without that branch.

Net: this is one of the stronger, more concretely specified ideas in this genre — real named tools, a real Make.com primitive (Data Store) doing real persistence work, a correct and non-generic agentic justification, and existing precedent for the pipeline shape. Feasible to wire up in a workshop if scoped to 1-2 competitors and the diff step is done via LLM-comparison rather than naive HTML diff. The only ding is the unspecified deal-owner data source for the optional branch, which is a minor scope note, not a rejection reason.

survivors.name: AI Web Researcher for Sales (account/pain-point brief before outreach)
survivors.trigger: New target account added to a prospecting list, or rep requests research on a named company
survivors.tools_touched: Web search/scraping tool -> company website + recent news -> LLM agent (multi-step reasoning: identifies business model, recent initiatives, likely pain points) -> structured brief output to Sheet/CRM note
survivors.autonomous_action: Given only a company name, autonomously plans and executes a multi-step research process (searches the web, reads the site, pulls recent news), reasons over the disparate sources to infer likely pain points and buying triggers, and writes a structured, outreach-ready brief — replacing 20-30 minutes of manual pre-call research per account.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: The model has no live knowledge of a specific company's current website content or this week's news; it must autonomously decide which pages/queries to pursue and synthesize across multiple fetched sources in sequence — a defining agentic (plan-then-act-then-synthesize) loop rather than a single completion.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: Medium — Make.com can chain a search API + scraper + OpenAI module, but true autonomous multi-step 'decide what to search next' looping is more naturally an n8n AI-agent node or Clay's Claygent; Make.com can approximate it with a fixed 2-3 step chain rather than open-ended agent planning.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: trigger is specific and dual-mode (new prospecting-list row added, or rep requests research on a named company) — both are real, watchable Make.com trigger types (Sheets row-added / form or Slack command). Tools are named at the correct altitude (search/scrape tool -> LLM reasoning step -> structured write-back to Sheet/CRM), not a vague category. Input is a single scalar (company name) and output is a defined artifact (structured, outreach-ready brief), not "insights" or "recommendations." This is far more specific than a hand-wavy pitch.

FEASIBLE on Make.com for a workshop: the pipeline decomposes cleanly into standard Make modules — a trigger (Sheets watch or Slack/form), an HTTP/scraper module for the company site, a second search-API call for recent news, an OpenAI/Anthropic module that receives both fetched blobs and reasons/synthesizes into a fixed-schema brief, and a Sheets/CRM write-back module. That's a 4-5 module build, in line with other workshop-scale automations, entirely no-code.

Importantly, the idea's own feasibility note is accurate rather than oversold: it correctly concedes Make.com can only approximate the "autonomous, open-ended re-planning" loop with a fixed 2-3 step chain (vs. n8n's AI Agent node or Clay's Claygent, which support true iterative "decide next query" looping). That's the honest, correct distinction — a workshop can still ship a useful, fixed-chain version of this (site content + one news query -> single LLM synthesis call) inside a session, even though it's technically "agentic-flavored" rather than a genuinely open-ended planning loop.

Residual gaps (implementation details, not disqualifying vagueness): Make.com has no native "web search" module, so the facilitator needs to pre-provision a specific search/scrape API (e.g., SerpAPI, a Make marketplace scraper app) and define how "recent news" is scoped (e.g., a dated query parameter) before the session — but these are prep-time specifics a facilitator resolves, not evidence the concept itself is hand-wavy.

survivors.name: Inbound Demo-Request Router with Calendly + Slack
survivors.trigger: New Calendly booking or contact-form submission
survivors.tools_touched: Calendly (or webform) -> ICP filter logic -> LLM (qualifies fit from submitted fields) -> Slack notification to the right rep/team -> HubSpot/CRM record creation -> conditional nurture sequence for non-ICP leads
survivors.autonomous_action: The moment a prospect books or submits a form, autonomously checks their answers/domain against ICP rules, routes qualified bookings straight to the correct rep's Slack channel with context, creates/updates the CRM contact, and for out-of-ICP submissions automatically enrolls them in a separate nurture flow instead of a sales rep's calendar — all before a human sees the lead.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: Real-time routing decisions depend on live form data plus ICP rules plus current rep availability/ownership mapping across three systems (Calendly, Slack, CRM) — this is a live branching pipeline triggered by an external event, not a text-completion task.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: High — Calendly, Slack, and most CRMs are first-class native Make.com integrations with dedicated modules and triggers; this is one of the most commonly built Make.com scenarios in practice.

verdict.reasoning:
Trigger: "New Calendly booking or contact-form submission" — specific and native to Make.com (Calendly has a dedicated instant trigger; webform submissions via Make's own webhook/form module or Typeform-style integrations are equally standard).

Tools: Calendly, Slack, HubSpot/CRM are all first-class Make.com modules with mature actions (create/update contact, post message to channel, etc.). The LLM step (qualify fit from submitted fields) is a single well-scoped classification/extraction call — exactly the kind of "text in, structured judgment out" task an LLM module handles well, not an overreach.

Action: The routing logic is concrete — ICP filter -> branch -> Slack post to specific channel with context OR CRM update -> nurture enrollment for non-ICP. This maps directly onto Make.com's router/filter primitives (a Router module with two filtered paths is the single most common Make.com pattern, matching the claim in "why_agentic_not_prompt" almost verbatim).

Feasibility check against workshop constraints:
- Live/webhook trigger: yes, Calendly webhook or Make's native webform trigger — no custom backend needed.
- Branching: yes, native Router + Filter, no code.
- LLM call: yes, single HTTP/OpenAI-style module, feasible in a 2-3 hour workshop slot.
- Slack "to the right rep" — this is the one soft spot: routing to a *dynamic* rep/channel based on ownership mapping requires either (a) a lookup table (Google Sheet/Airtable mapped to rep-to-Slack-channel) or (b) hardcoded logic. This is very buildable no-code (Google Sheets lookup is a standard Make module) but the proposal doesn't explicitly name that lookup mechanism — it says "current rep availability/ownership mapping across three systems" as justification for complexity, which in a live demo would need to be simplified to a static or Sheet-based mapping. That's a simplification note, not a feasibility blocker — the "even if simplified" clause in the question explicitly allows for this.
- CRM creation: HubSpot module natively supports create-or-update contact; feasible.
- Nurture sequence enrollment: HubSpot workflows can be triggered via API/native Make module (add to list/workflow) — feasible, though this piece could be simplified to "tag contact" in a workshop cut instead of a full nurture sequence, which is a reasonable simplification.

Nothing here is vague — every box names a specific trigger, specific named tools with specific actions (not "some CRM", not "notify someone"), and a specific branching decision. The claimed source_url resolves to a real, well-documented Make.com integration page (Calendly + Slack is indeed one of the most common templates in Make's library), supporting the feasibility claim rather than being a fabricated citation.

Compare against anti-patterns: this is not "an agent that handles customer support" (vague category) or "automate marketing" (hand-wavy). It names the exact trigger event, the exact sequence of module types, and the exact branch outcomes. The one thing to flag for the workshop facilitator is to pre-build the rep-to-channel mapping (Google Sheet or hardcoded router filter) rather than promising true "live availability" sync, since real-time calendar-availability-based routing would need an extra API layer Make doesn't do natively out of the box — but the core routing-by-ICP-rules-to-a-channel pattern remains fully native and highly feasible.

Verdict: concrete and feasible, with one minor scope note (simplify "availability mapping" to a static lookup table for the workshop, not a blocker).

survivors.name: Resume Screening & Scoring Agent (Google Drive → PDF.co → AI → Sheets)
survivors.trigger: New resume file (PDF/DOCX) lands in a watched Google Drive folder (or arrives as an email attachment / form submission / ATS webhook)
survivors.tools_touched: Google Drive, PDF.co (PDF-to-JSON conversion), HTTP module, LLM (GPT-4/Gemini) via Make AI Agent, Google Sheets
survivors.autonomous_action: Converts the resume to structured text, evaluates it against 4 predefined screening questions/criteria, assigns a 0-2 score per answer with a short explanation, sums a total score, and appends a fully populated row (contact info, per-question scores, rationale, total) to a ranked candidate spreadsheet — no human touches an individual resume until the ranked list exists.
survivors.why_agentic_not_prompt: Requires chaining a file-system watcher, a document-conversion API, a structured LLM judgment step, and a database write — each step depends on the live output of the previous one (file arrival is unpredictable, conversion output varies per resume format), so it can't be a single static prompt; it's a persistent, multi-tool, multi-step pipeline that runs unattended every time a new file appears.
survivors.make_com_feasibility: high — this is a published, ready-made Make.com template (Google Drive + PDF.co + AI Agent + Sheets), documented step-by-step by Make itself.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: The trigger is specific (Google Drive watched-folder file arrival, with named fallback triggers), the tools are named exactly rather than gestured at (Google Drive, PDF.co PDF-to-JSON conversion, HTTP module, Make AI Agent/LLM, Google Sheets), and the autonomous action is fully specified — convert resume to structured JSON, score against 4 fixed criteria on a 0-2 scale with rationale, sum total, append one populated row (contact info + per-question scores + rationale + total) to a ranked sheet. This is a precise pipeline spec, not a vague category like "use AI to screen resumes."

FEASIBLE: I fetched the cited source (https://www.make.com/en/how-to-guides/ai-recruiting-agent) directly to verify rather than taking the claim at face value. It confirms a real, published, step-documented Make.com template matching the proposal almost exactly: Google Drive watch-folder trigger → Google Drive download/convert → PDF.co Convert-from-PDF (JSON2 type) → HTTP GET to retrieve the JSON → Make AI Agent scoring 4 questions at 0-2 each with explanations → Google Sheets Add-a-Row with name/email/LinkedIn/answers/scores/total. The why_agentic_not_prompt justification is also sound on the merits (independent of the memorized template): file arrival is async/unpredictable, PDF.co's conversion output varies per resume format, and a structured LLM judgment step feeding a deterministic spreadsheet write genuinely requires chaining live tool outputs — it cannot collapse into a single static prompt.

Caveats noted but not disqualifying: PDF.co is a separate paid third-party API needing its own signup/API key (extra setup tax for a workshop audience beyond Make + Google accounts), and the real template is actually built as two linked Make scenarios (Drive/PDF.co/AI in one, Sheets-append in the other), which the proposal's tools_touched list doesn't surface — a facilitator should budget time for both. Net: this is one of the strongest, most standard indie-hacker Make.com patterns (as the submission itself notes) — comparable in build complexity to well-known "scheduled digest" recipes that are widely documented in Make's own template library. It clears the concrete+feasible bar cleanly.

One minor inaccuracy: in the source, Linkup itself does the synthesis and OpenAI is only an optional extension for email drafting, not the stated synthesis engine — but substituting an explicit OpenAI/LLM module for that synthesis step in the Make.com port is a trivial, workshop-appropriate simplification that doesn't affect feasibility.

FEASIBLE on Make.com: Apollo.io and Linkup have no native Make.com modules but both expose standard REST APIs callable via Make's generic HTTP module (a bog-standard pattern), OpenAI has a first-class native Make module, and Make's linear scenario model is exactly suited to chaining sequential API outputs into a prompt and then to a write-back module (Google Sheets/Docs/HubSpot/Airtable all natively supported). Realistic workshop build is ~4-5 modules. The one real cost is needing three separate API credentials (Apollo, Linkup, OpenAI) pre-provisioned to avoid burning live workshop time on signups — a logistics caveat, not an infeasibility. Also worth flagging as a caveat (not a build blocker): LinkedIn-profile-reading APIs like Linkup sit in a ToS/reliability gray zone for production use, though this doesn't block wiring up a workshop demo.

allIdeas.name: Intent-Signal Triggered Outbound (job-change / funding-alert agent)
allIdeas.trigger: External signal fires: a tracked contact changes jobs (LinkedIn/Sales Nav alert or Clay signal), or a target account raises funding (Crunchbase webhook/RSS)
allIdeas.tools_touched: Crunchbase or LinkedIn signal feed -> Clay (or Apollo) enrichment waterfall -> LLM (drafts personalized opener referencing the specific trigger event) -> CRM write (HubSpot/Salesforce) -> Slack alert to account owner
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Watches for the trigger event continuously, when it fires autonomously enriches the new/changed contact, generates outreach copy that explicitly references the funding round or new role, updates the CRM record, and pings the owning rep in Slack — end-to-end from signal to rep-ready message in under a minute with zero manual monitoring.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: Depends on an event the LLM cannot know about until a live feed reports it, requires multi-tool chaining (signal source -> enrichment -> CRM -> Slack) and timing-sensitive autonomous execution — a prompt is static text, not a thing that watches the world and fires itself.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: High — Make.com supports RSS/webhook watchers for Crunchbase-style feeds, has native HubSpot/Salesforce and Slack modules, and Clay itself pushes into Make via webhook, so this is a well-trodden combination.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, clearly. The trigger (job-change alert or Crunchbase funding webhook), tools (Crunchbase/LinkedIn -> Clay/Apollo -> LLM -> HubSpot/Salesforce -> Slack), and action (enrich, draft trigger-referencing copy, write CRM, alert rep) are all specific and non-vague. This clears the bar the batch is screening for.

FEASIBLE FOR A LIVE WORKSHOP: No, not as specified — the 'High' feasibility claim overstates it. Two dependency-layer problems undercut it:
(1) LinkedIn has no public API/webhook for job-change or Sales Navigator alerts; the only ways to get that data are manual export or scraping, which violates LinkedIn's ToS — not something to wire live in a workshop.
(2) Crunchbase's funding webhook/RSS feed used for alerting is gated behind an Enterprise API tier, not a free/trial signal a workshop can provision in-session. Clay's own site (fetched directly) confirms job-change and funding signals exist as a product feature but does not document a Make.com/webhook integration path in the cited source, meaning the chain also assumes a paid Clay workspace with webhook egress.

Net effect: the downstream half of the pipeline (LLM drafting -> CRM write -> Slack alert) is genuinely Make.com-native and easy to demo. But the trigger half (real external signal firing) cannot actually be connected live without paid/enterprise accounts or ToS violations. A workshop version would need to substitute a simulated trigger (e.g., a manually-updated Google Sheet row or dummy RSS feed standing in for 'funding round detected') rather than the real Crunchbase/LinkedIn signal the idea describes — which is a modification the write-up doesn't acknowledge. As written, it should be rejected/flagged rather than accepted as directly buildable.

allIdeas.name: LinkedIn Lead-Gen, Scoring & Multi-Channel Outreach Agent
allIdeas.trigger: Scheduled run (e.g., weekly) or manual kickoff with an ICP description
allIdeas.tools_touched: LinkedIn/Sales Navigator scraping (via Bright Data or similar) -> Google Sheets (central lead database) -> AI agent (scores lead against ICP, drafts messaging) -> outputs: LinkedIn connection request text, HTML email, and a third channel message
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Takes a plain-language ICP description, autonomously finds matching LinkedIn profiles, writes them to a Sheet, scores/prioritizes each one, and generates three distinct personalized outreach drafts (LinkedIn DM, email, and a third channel) per lead — a full ICP-to-outreach-ready pipeline run without a human doing the searching or drafting.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: Needs live web/LinkedIn data the model doesn't have, a scoring step with persistent state (the Sheet as memory across runs), and generation of multiple distinct artifacts per lead — this is a multi-stage pipeline with external actions, not a single completion.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: Medium-high — the AI scoring/drafting and Google Sheets legs are trivial in Make.com; the LinkedIn scraping leg typically needs a scraping API partner (Bright Data, PhantomBuster) since Make has no native LinkedIn scraper, which is the one added-cost/complexity point.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: mostly yes. Trigger (scheduled/manual + ICP text input), tools (Google Sheets, LLM scoring/drafting step, LinkedIn scraping via named vendor category), and outputs (LinkedIn DM, HTML email, plus one more channel, per lead) are all specifically named rather than a vague category like 'an outreach agent.' One soft spot: 'a third channel message' is left unspecified (SMS? WhatsApp? X DM?) — a real but minor gap.

FEASIBILITY: fails as literally scoped for a live workshop, for one dominant reason. I fetched the cited source (n8n.io workflow 3490) directly: it explicitly states the workflow 'requires a self-hosted n8n instance with the AnySite LinkedIn community node; it cannot run on n8n.cloud.' That is a much stronger red flag than the proposal's own framing ('Make has no native LinkedIn scraper, which is the one added-cost/complexity point') suggests. In practice, live LinkedIn/Sales Navigator scraping via Bright Data or PhantomBuster in front of a workshop audience means: a paid scraper account must be pre-provisioned, LinkedIn's bot detection/rate limits/CAPTCHAs can break the demo live, session-cookie auth is fiddly to set up in the room, and scraping LinkedIn at all raises ToS/legal exposure that a founder-ops workshop should surface, not wave past. The Sheets leg and the LLM scoring/drafting leg are genuinely trivial in Make.com and not in question.

Additionally, three named integration legs (scraper API, Sheets, LLM) generating three distinct per-lead artifacts is a lot of live-build surface for a typical workshop time box; the reference implementation itself needed a non-cloud workaround just to function, which the proposal's feasibility rating ('Medium-high') understates.

Net: buildable and demonstrable only if explicitly simplified — e.g., replace live LinkedIn scraping with a pre-seeded CSV of sample profiles for the live build, treat the scraper integration as 'described, not live-demoed,' and pin the vague third channel to one concrete choice. As submitted, the idea overstates ease on its riskiest and most legally sensitive leg, so it does not clear the bar as a ready-to-wire workshop exercise.

allIdeas.name: Meeting-Notes-to-CRM Autopilot (Fireflies/Gong-style)
allIdeas.trigger: A sales call ends (calendar event with a recording bot joins Zoom/Meet/Teams)
allIdeas.tools_touched: Fireflies or Gong (transcription + summarization) -> LLM (extracts action items, objections, next steps, deal-stage signals) -> CRM (HubSpot/Salesforce field/stage update) -> Slack (routes summary to deal owner/channel)
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Automatically records and transcribes the call, extracts structured fields (objections raised, commitments made, suggested next deal stage) via LLM reasoning over the transcript, writes those fields directly into the CRM deal record, and routes a summary to Slack — with zero manual note-taking or CRM data entry by the rep.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: Requires audio capture and transcription infrastructure, a retrieval step over a long transcript, structured extraction mapped to specific CRM schema fields, and a write-back action to a third system — a prompt has no transcript to read and no CRM API access on its own.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: High — Fireflies has a native Zapier/webhook + GraphQL API that Make.com can call directly; CRM and Slack modules are native Make.com connectors, making this one of the more turnkey builds.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, clearly. The trigger is specific (calendar event with a recording bot joining Zoom/Meet/Teams, firing Fireflies' "Transcription complete" webhook), not a vague "when a call happens." Tools are named precisely — Fireflies GraphQL API/webhook, not a generic "transcription tool" — with named CRM targets (HubSpot/Salesforce) and named output fields (objections raised, commitments made, suggested next deal stage). This is a fully specified pipeline, not a hand-wavy category.

FEASIBLE on Make.com: Verified via web search that all the load-bearing technical claims check out:
- Fireflies has a real webhook (x-hub-signature HMAC-verified) firing on "Transcription complete," and Make.com has a native Fireflies.ai app/connector plus generic HTTP/GraphQL module support (make.com/en/integrations/fireflies-ai).
- Fireflies' calendar auto-join into Zoom/Meet/Teams is a real, documented feature (guide.fireflies.ai), not invented.
- Make.com has long-standing native HubSpot and Salesforce connectors with deal/record update modules, and a native Slack message module — these are some of the most mature connectors on the platform.

One real gap the pitch glosses over, which keeps this from being a flawless plan but doesn't sink feasibility: the trigger ("a sales call ends") can't be manually fired in a workshop the way a form submission or button-click can — you'd need either a pre-recorded/pre-transcribed sample call in Fireflies, or to simulate by hand-feeding a saved transcript into the LLM→CRM→Slack half of the scenario. This is a standard, easy workaround (skip live trigger, demo from a canned transcript) but the write-up doesn't flag it, presenting the live-call trigger as if it's workshop-demoable as-is. Also assumes attendees already have HubSpot/Salesforce/Slack provisioned with admin API access, which is a fair "bring your own stack" assumption for this workshop genre but a real prerequisite. Neither issue changes the verdict — the idea is concrete and the connectors are real and native — but the trigger-simulation workaround should be called out explicitly when presented to founders so no one is surprised mid-build.

allIdeas.name: Deal Pipeline Watcher / Stagnation Flagger
allIdeas.trigger: Daily scheduled scan of all open CRM deals
allIdeas.tools_touched: CRM API (HubSpot/Salesforce/Pipedrive) -> LLM (reasons over last-activity-date, stage, deal value to classify risk) -> Slack/email digest to rep or founder
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Runs every day without being asked, cross-references each open deal's last-touch date and stage against expected velocity, autonomously classifies which deals have gone quiet or are unusually hot, and pushes a prioritized daily digest so the founder/rep only spends time on deals the system flagged — replacing a manual weekly pipeline review.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: The judgment ('this deal is stagnating') depends on live, per-deal state compared against a moving baseline (time elapsed, activity count) that must be recomputed daily by querying the CRM — there is no fixed prompt input since the entire pipeline changes every day.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: High — a Make.com scenario with a daily scheduler trigger, a CRM 'search records' module, an iterator, an OpenAI module for the risk classification, and a digest email/Slack module is a standard, well-supported pattern.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, on all three required dimensions.
- Trigger: specific and unambiguous — "daily scheduled scan of all open CRM deals" maps directly to a Make.com scheduler module (interval trigger) feeding a CRM search/list module. Not vague ("periodically check things").
- Tools: named concretely — HubSpot/Salesforce/Pipedrive as the CRM source (all three have first-party or well-supported Make.com modules), an LLM step (OpenAI module) for classification, and Slack/email for output. Each hop in the chain is a real, nameable Make.com module, not a hand-waved "integrate with CRM."
- Action: specific and falsifiable — cross-reference last-activity-date + stage + deal value against an expected-velocity baseline, classify into a risk bucket (stagnating vs hot), and push a prioritized digest. This is a well-defined transformation, not "analyze the pipeline" left undefined.

FEASIBLE for a no-code Make.com workshop build, even simplified:
- Scheduler module: native, trivial.
- CRM search/list module: HubSpot, Pipedrive, and Salesforce all have mature Make.com apps with a "Search/List Deals" or equivalent action returning stage, last-activity timestamp, and amount — exactly the three fields the logic needs. This is standard, heavily-documented Make.com territory (the cited make.com/en/solutions/automate-sales page is a legitimate, on-topic source, not a stretch citation).
- Iterator: native Make.com module, standard pattern for looping over an array of deals returned by a search.
- OpenAI module for classification: native Make.com OpenAI app, "Create a Completion/Chat Completion" action — feeding it per-deal fields (days since last touch, stage, value) and asking for a risk label + one-line reason is a bounded, well-scoped prompt. This is squarely the kind of judgment call an LLM step is good at and a fixed rule engine would need constant retuning for (variable expected velocity per stage/deal size).
- Aggregator + digest: Make.com's "Array Aggregator" or simple text aggregation into a Slack message/email module — standard, no custom code needed.
- Realistic simplification for a workshop: cap it at one CRM (e.g., Pipedrive test account, easiest sandbox to spin up), a handful of seeded fake deals, and skip nuanced velocity baselining in favor of a simple "days since last activity > threshold" rule combined with the LLM step for the qualitative "hot deal" judgment and prioritized write-up. That's buildable live in a 60-90 minute session.

Why this passes the "agentic, not prompt" bar: the reasoning target (which deals are stagnating) depends on live, per-deal state pulled fresh from the CRM every run, not a static prompt — this justifies the tool-calling/data-fetch architecture rather than a single canned prompt, consistent with the stated rationale.

Minor caveats (not disqualifying): "expected velocity per stage" implies a benchmark table that isn't specified — in a workshop this would need to be simplified to a flat day-threshold or a small hardcoded per-stage table, which the idea's own feasibility note implicitly allows for. Also, Salesforce's API/module setup has more friction (OAuth app approval, sandbox access) than HubSpot/Pipedrive for a live workshop, so the facilitator should steer toward Pipedrive or HubSpot as the demo CRM rather than presenting all three as equally easy — but this is an implementation detail, not a concreteness/feasibility failure of the idea itself.

allIdeas.name: CRM Data Hygiene / Deduplication Agent
allIdeas.trigger: Scheduled sweep (e.g., nightly) of new and existing CRM contact/company records
allIdeas.tools_touched: CRM export/API -> enrichment waterfall (Clearbit/Apollo/People Data Labs) -> LLM (fuzzy-matches likely duplicates, flags stale titles/companies from job-change signals) -> CRM write-back (merge suggestion or auto-update)
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Continuously re-verifies contact accuracy (title, employer, email validity) against fresh enrichment data, autonomously flags or merges likely-duplicate records, and updates stale fields — addressing the documented ~25-30%/year CRM contact-accuracy decay without a human running manual list-cleaning exercises.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: Deduplication and staleness detection require comparing many live records against external data sources and each other (a retrieval + comparison problem), then conditionally writing updates back — this is inherently multi-record, multi-tool, and stateful, not answerable from a single prompt.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: Medium — logic is straightforward in Make.com (scheduler, CRM search, enrichment HTTP call, OpenAI comparison, conditional update), but at high contact volumes this can hit Make's per-scenario operation/row limits and may need batching.

verdict.reasoning:
The idea has genuinely concrete elements — named tools (Clearbit/Apollo/PDL), a specific trigger (nightly scheduler), and a plausible Make.com module chain (scheduler → CRM search → HTTP enrichment call → OpenAI comparison → conditional update). That part is real, not hand-wavy.

But it fails on two grounds that matter for a workshop build:

1. Feasibility is self-admittedly shaky, not just "medium." The proposal itself flags per-scenario operation/row limits and the need for batching at "high contact volumes" — but a nightly full-CRM sweep with an enrichment waterfall (3 chained paid APIs) against "new AND existing" records is exactly a high-volume, multi-record iteration pattern. That's not a workshop-simplifiable edge case; it's the core mechanic of the workflow. A no-code demo needs to either fake this (dummy 10-row sheet — cheapens the "autonomous CRM hygiene" pitch) or hit real limits live. Fuzzy-match deduplication across many-to-many record pairs (comparing N records against each other, not against one external source) is also a genuinely awkward fit for Make's linear/iterator paradigm — it typically wants a real dedup library or vector similarity step, not an LLM call per pair.

2. The autonomous_action overreaches into "auto-merge" / "auto-update" CRM records unattended. Silently merging or overwriting live CRM data based on LLM fuzzy-matching is a high-blast-radius, hard-to-reverse action (data loss/corruption risk) — not something to demo as "autonomous" in a founder workshop without heavy guardrails (human approval step, staging table, audit log), which the spec doesn't include. This makes the "why_agentic" framing (multi-tool, stateful, conditional writes) accurate as a description, but the write-back path as specified is riskier than what a workshop should model as a wire-it-yourself pattern.

Additional flags: 
- source_url is a placeholder (default.com) — the "~25-30%/year decay" stat is unsourced/possibly fabricated, which is a hard no per grounding rules.
- Three paid enrichment APIs chained in a waterfall adds real cost/API-key setup friction for a live workshop session, beyond typical no-code demo scope.

Net: concrete on paper, but not feasible to wire up safely and completely in a workshop without simplifying away the actual hard/interesting parts (multi-record fuzzy dedup, write-back safety, volume handling) — at which point it stops being the workflow described. Recommend rejecting as-is; a workshop-safe variant would scope to a small static list, read-only flagging (no auto-write), and a single enrichment source, with the decay stat either sourced or dropped.

allIdeas.name: Competitor & Market Intelligence Digest for Sales Talking Points
allIdeas.trigger: Scheduled crawl (daily/weekly) of competitor websites, pricing pages, and news sources
allIdeas.tools_touched: Firecrawl or Bright Data (scrapes competitor sites/pricing pages) -> diff/change-detection logic -> LLM (analyzes what changed and drafts sales talking points) -> Slack digest to sales team, optionally triggers a sub-workflow tied to specific open deals
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Autonomously re-scrapes competitor pages on a schedule, detects meaningful changes (price drop, new feature, news mention) versus the last snapshot, has the LLM interpret the significance and draft rep-ready talking points, and delivers a formatted digest — and can trigger a targeted alert to reps with open deals against that specific competitor.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: Needs persistent state (yesterday's page snapshot vs today's) to detect a *change*, live scraping the model has no access to, and conditional downstream branching to specific deal owners — a prompt has no memory of prior page state and can't crawl the web itself.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: High — Make.com's HTTP/Firecrawl modules plus a data-store module (to hold the last snapshot for diffing) plus OpenAI and Slack modules cover this end to end; this exact shape exists as a published n8n template.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE — yes, on every axis:
- Trigger is specific: scheduled crawl (daily/weekly) of named target types (competitor websites, pricing pages, news sources), not "monitor the market."
- Tools are named products, not categories: Firecrawl/Bright Data for scraping, a diff/change-detection step, an LLM step, Slack for delivery, plus an optional sub-workflow branch to deal owners. Each maps to a real Make.com module class (HTTP/Firecrawl app module, Data Store module for snapshot persistence, OpenAI module, Slack module, Router/Filter for branching).
- Action is a well-defined pipeline, not a vague "keep sales informed": scrape -> diff against last snapshot -> LLM interprets significance -> drafts rep-ready talking points -> Slack digest -> optional targeted alert to reps with open deals against that competitor. That's five concrete stages with clear inputs/outputs at each hop.
- The "why agentic not prompt" justification is correctly reasoned, not hand-wavy: it correctly identifies the two things a bare prompt genuinely cannot do — hold persistent state across runs (yesterday's snapshot) and reach out to fetch live web content — and ties the conditional branching (deal-owner routing) to needing workflow logic, not just a smarter prompt. This is a legitimate agentic justification, unlike degenerate "summarize this text" cases dressed up as agents.

FEASIBLE on Make.com in a workshop setting — with caveats worth flagging but not disqualifying:
- Scraping: Firecrawl has a native Make.com app/module; Bright Data can be wired via HTTP module. Either works in a 2-3 hour workshop slot for 1-2 competitor URLs.
- Diff/state: Make.com's Data Store module is real and commonly used exactly for this pattern (store last snapshot, compare on next run) — this is not an invented feature.
- LLM step: standard OpenAI module, trivial.
- Delivery: Slack module, trivial.
- Precedent: the cited n8n template (n8n.io/workflows/3101) demonstrates this exact shape has been built and published before, which is reasonable corroborating evidence the pipeline shape is sound — though it's an n8n template, not a Make.com one, so "this exact shape exists as a published n8n template" is true as stated but shouldn't be overstated as proof of Make.com feasibility; it's evidence of the *logical* pipeline's soundness, and Make.com has equivalent primitives (HTTP/Firecrawl, Data Store, OpenAI, Slack, Router) to reproduce it.

Workshop-simplification risks (real, but scope down rather than kill the idea):
- Full diffing (structured price/feature diff, not just raw HTML diff) usually needs a semantic diff step or an LLM-as-differ rather than naive text diff, since pricing pages have lots of noise (session tokens, timestamps, ads) that would trigger false positives on a raw HTML compare. In a workshop, this is best simplified to "LLM reads old snapshot + new snapshot text and decides if there's a meaningful change" rather than a byte-level diff — the proposal already gestures at this ("LLM analyzes what changed"), so it's compatible, just needs the facilitator to steer learners away from naive HTML diffing.
- Scraping is legally/ToS gray for some competitor sites (bot-blocking, robots.txt) — a workshop caveat, not a design flaw.
- The "sub-workflow tied to specific open deals" branch implies a CRM data source (deal owner mapping) that isn't named in tools_touched — this is the one soft spot: it's plausible (a Google Sheet or lightweight CRM lookup) but the proposal doesn't specify where "open deals against that competitor" data lives. This should be simplified/flagged in the workshop as "maintain a simple Sheet mapping competitor -> deal owner" rather than assuming a full CRM integration — but it doesn't break the core digest workflow, which stands alone even without that branch.

Net: this is one of the stronger, more concretely specified ideas in this genre — real named tools, a real Make.com primitive (Data Store) doing real persistence work, a correct and non-generic agentic justification, and existing precedent for the pipeline shape. Feasible to wire up in a workshop if scoped to 1-2 competitors and the diff step is done via LLM-comparison rather than naive HTML diff. The only ding is the unspecified deal-owner data source for the optional branch, which is a minor scope note, not a rejection reason.

allIdeas.name: Proposal/Contract Generation & No-Response Follow-up Agent
allIdeas.trigger: Deal reaches 'proposal' stage in CRM, or a sent proposal has had no activity for N days
allIdeas.tools_touched: CRM (deal/customer data) -> PandaDoc (template population: pricing, scope, customer segment logic) -> e-signature tracking -> LLM (drafts reminder email/LinkedIn message copy) -> CRM stage update
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Auto-generates a proposal document from CRM data (pulling the right pricing tier and scope for that customer segment), sends it for signature, monitors view/sign activity, and if there's no response after a set window autonomously sends a follow-up reminder (email or LinkedIn) and logs the nudge — closing the loop between 'proposal sent' and 'signed' without a rep manually tracking it.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: Requires document-state polling (has it been viewed/signed?) over time, conditional branching on elapsed time with no response, and write actions across CRM + document platform + messaging channel — none of which a single-shot prompt can observe or execute.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: Medium-high — PandaDoc has native Make.com integration for document creation/status webhooks; the delay/no-response branch is a standard Make.com pattern (webhook + sleep/scheduled re-check + router), though PandaDoc's per-document webhook granularity needs to be tested for the specific 'no view after N days' condition.

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: Yes, on the trigger/tools/action axis this is specific — named CRM stage trigger, named tool (PandaDoc), named branching logic (elapsed time + no signature → nudge), specific channels (email/LinkedIn). It is not a vague "automate sales" category pitch.

FEASIBLE for a workshop: No, or at best "medium" mis-rated as "medium-high." Two concrete problems surfaced on verification:

1. Source URL doesn't support the claim. https://www.pandadoc.com/features/collaborate/contract-automation/ never mentions Make.com — it names Zapier, HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Stripe, Slack as its integration partners. Citing this URL as the source for "PandaDoc has native Make.com integration" is a mismatch between citation and claim — the grounding rule (verify before claiming) is violated here, since the linked page doesn't back the specific technical assertion the idea rests on.

2. Make.com's actual PandaDoc app (apps.make.com/pandadoc) does have a native "Watch Documents" webhook trigger with a "State changed" event — so document lifecycle tracking is technically possible. But this is thinner than the idea implies: (a) it requires a paid PandaDoc plan with webhooks enabled under Integrations > Webhooks — an extra paid-tier dependency to disclose in a workshop, not something you can demo on a free/trial account; (b) "state changed" fires on any status transition (sent → viewed → completed), it is not itself a "no activity for N days" signal. The "no-response after N days" branch the idea describes is not a native trigger at all — it has to be hand-built as a scheduled/polling flow (Make.com scheduler re-checking document status via "Get a Document" on an interval, comparing timestamps, and branching), which the idea's own feasibility note gestures at ("delay/no-response branch is a standard Make.com pattern") but understates as a "webhook + sleep" pattern — Make.com has no sleep/delay-then-recheck primitive against a webhook payload the way described; it would need a separate scheduled scenario polling PandaDoc's document list/status API and diffing against last-known state, which is a second scenario with its own state-storage problem (Data Store to remember "last nudged at X"), not a single flow.

Net: the core "generate proposal from CRM data with correct pricing tier/scope logic" leg is very plausible on Make.com (CRM trigger → PandaDoc create-document with templated fields is a bread-and-butter integration). But the "monitor for no response after N days and autonomously follow up" leg — which is the part that makes this "agentic" per the idea's own justification — is the weakest link: it requires (a) a paid PandaDoc tier for webhooks, (b) a second polling scenario with a Data Store to track elapsed time, and (c) writing back to CRM + sending a LinkedIn message (LinkedIn has no public API/Make.com module for sending messages — this leg is not automatable at all via Make.com and would silently degrade to a manual step or an email-only fallback, which the idea doesn't flag).

Verdict: reject as written. The idea is directionally sound and a scoped-down version (CRM → PandaDoc doc generation, plus a same-scenario "check again in N days" using Make's built-in scheduler + Data Store, email-only follow-up, dropping the LinkedIn leg) would be workshop-feasible. As submitted, it overstates feasibility (cites a source that doesn't back the Make.com claim, glosses over the paid-webhook requirement, invents a "sleep" primitive Make.com doesn't have for this pattern, and includes a LinkedIn-send action with no feasible no-code path). Recommend sending back for revision: fix the source citation, drop or caveat the LinkedIn channel, and describe the no-response check as a second polling scenario with a Data Store rather than implying a single webhook-driven flow handles it.

allIdeas.name: AI Web Researcher for Sales (account/pain-point brief before outreach)
allIdeas.trigger: New target account added to a prospecting list, or rep requests research on a named company
allIdeas.tools_touched: Web search/scraping tool -> company website + recent news -> LLM agent (multi-step reasoning: identifies business model, recent initiatives, likely pain points) -> structured brief output to Sheet/CRM note
allIdeas.autonomous_action: Given only a company name, autonomously plans and executes a multi-step research process (searches the web, reads the site, pulls recent news), reasons over the disparate sources to infer likely pain points and buying triggers, and writes a structured, outreach-ready brief — replacing 20-30 minutes of manual pre-call research per account.
allIdeas.why_agentic_not_prompt: The model has no live knowledge of a specific company's current website content or this week's news; it must autonomously decide which pages/queries to pursue and synthesize across multiple fetched sources in sequence — a defining agentic (plan-then-act-then-synthesize) loop rather than a single completion.
allIdeas.make_com_feasibility: Medium — Make.com can chain a search API + scraper + OpenAI module, but true autonomous multi-step 'decide what to search next' looping is more naturally an n8n AI-agent node or Clay's Claygent; Make.com can approximate it with a fixed 2-3 step chain rather than open-ended agent planning.

This is infrastructure setup, not a workflow-building exercise, and it's exactly the kind of dependency that eats an entire session on API keys and account provisioning rather than teaching agent-building concepts.

4. Compare to the S2-canon-style bar already established for this user's other workshops (HR Candidate Screener, 3 nodes, as the cohort-actual artifact) — that's the calibration for "what's buildable live." Verdict: concrete, yes. Feasible to actually wire up live in a workshop setting (even simplified) — no. The resume-scoring half (Notion trigger → Gemini score → conditional notify) is workshop-feasible on its own and could be extracted as a smaller, honest artifact; the voice-interview half should be presented as an architecture case study / n8n template walkthrough rather than something participants build live on Make.com.

allIdeas.name: Warm-Intro Path Finder Agent

allIdeas.tools_touched: Clay (LinkedIn 'People Also Viewed'/network enrichment) + founder's LinkedIn connections + CRM

verdict.reasoning:
CONCRETE: partially yes, partially no.
- Trigger is genuinely concrete (new CRM row / manual batch run before a sprint).
- Tools named are specific (Clay, CRM, LinkedIn), and the source URL is real and verifiable — I fetched it via search (direct WebFetch 404'd, likely transient/blocked) and confirmed Clay's blog documents exactly this "People Also Viewed" (PAV) technique for surfacing warm-intro paths. So this isn't a hallucinated citation, which is a genuine strength.
- BUT the `autonomous_action` field materially overstates what the underlying technique does. It describes "cross-referencing the founder's existing network" against each investor's network as if it's a clean two-graph intersection ("mutual connections"). The real Clay technique explicitly is NOT mutual-connection scraping — the source blog says scraping true mutual connections "doesn't work at scale" and is why Clay uses PAV as a proxy instead (people who "actually know" the target, sourced from LinkedIn's recommendation algorithm, not a graph traversal against the founder's own connection list). So the idea's core mechanism claim is a subtly inaccurate simplification of its own cited source — it's describing a more powerful/cleaner capability (real graph cross-referencing) than what Clay/LinkedIn actually offer. That's a "vague-dressed-as-precise" problem: specific nouns (Clay, PAV, CRM) wrapped around an action description that doesn't match how the tool actually works.
- "Ranks the best warm-intro path" and "drafts an intro-request message" are appropriately concrete LLM-step asks, no complaint there.

FEASIBILITY on Make.com in a workshop:
- Clay is not a simple API call founders can hit in a 2-3 hour workshop slot — it requires its own paid seat, credit-based enrichment runs, and PAV enrichment is one of Clay's pricier/rate-limited "AI-powered" columns. Provisioning Clay accounts + LinkedIn connection sync + CRM integration for a workshop cohort is a heavy pre-req, not a "simplified but feasible" no-code build.
- Getting the founder's own LinkedIn connections list into any tool programmatically is itself hard: LinkedIn has no public API for exporting a personal connections list (Sales Navigator's API is restricted/partner-gated; the CSV export is manual, static, and would need to be re-uploaded each time — not something Make.com can pull live on a trigger). So the "trigger: new investor added to CRM" firing an automatic re-cross-reference against "founder's existing network" is not actually wireable without a recurring manual CSV re-upload step — undermining the "automatic" framing in the very name of the agent.
- Make.com's role here is thin (webhook passthrough + LLM ranking step + Slack/email draft) — that part is fine and standard — but the feasibility rating of "Medium" undersells that the hard part (Clay account + LinkedIn network export + PAV credits) sits entirely outside Make.com's or the workshop's control, and is exactly the kind of dependency that stalls a live build.
- Net: for a workshop meant to have founders build and see something work same-day, this has a real risk of turning into "watch me explain why the LinkedIn export step doesn't work live" rather than a completed build. A simplified stand-in (e.g., founder manually pastes a static CSV of connections once, skip live LinkedIn/Sales Nav entirely) could rescue it, but as written the idea assumes live/automatic network access that doesn't exist.

Verdict: Reject as currently specified. It is concrete on trigger/tools naming and has a real (non-fabricated) source, but the core "autonomous action" mischaracterizes what the cited technique actually does (proxy signal, not true graph cross-referencing), and the feasibility rating glosses over a hard, workshop-breaking dependency: there is no live/automatable way to pull a founder's LinkedIn connections into Make.com or Clay on a recurring trigger. This needs to be rewritten as either (a) a one-time-CSV-upload + Clay PAV lookup + LLM ranking (batch, not "new CRM row" triggered), with the mutual-connection language corrected to "PAV-based proxy signal," or (b) swapped for a domain where the data access is actually programmatic.

FEASIBLE ON MAKE.COM IN A WORKSHOP: no, and the idea's own feasibility note underplays the real blocker.

1. Auth is the actual problem, not just "no native app." The idea states "no native Mercury/Brex Make.com app, so uses generic HTTP/webhook modules" as if that's a minor downgrade from a pre-built connector. In practice, wiring this up requires a real, live Mercury or Brex API token/OAuth credential tied to an actual funded business bank account. None of the ~10 founders in this room can be assumed to (a) bank with Mercury or Brex specifically, (b) have API access enabled on their account (often gated behind account tier or a support request), or (c) want to paste live banking credentials into a laptop during a shared workshop. 2. The "calculation" step is glossed over. Turning raw balance/transaction pulls into a defensible "burn rate" and "runway in months" isn't a one-module math step — it needs trailing-N-month averaging and exclusion of one-time inflows (e.g., the last funding round itself would make burn look negative/nonsensical if not filtered out), plus reliable spend-category data that Mercury/Brex APIs don't cleanly expose. Session-context problem: per this project's own source-of-truth doc, the workshop's build tool was already superseded from Make.com to Hermes Agent, and the actual live-build candidates under consideration are Investor Update / Investor Outreach agents — this Runway/Burn idea is one candidate in a Round-2 catalog being screened, not a chosen build. Verdict: reject as specified. A same-day-feasible variant would swap Mercury/Brex for a Google Sheet founders maintain themselves, or Stripe (more commonly held, better-scoped read-only keys) as the data source. As written, this requires a mandatory pre-workshop credential/sandbox setup step and should not be treated as a live, same-session build.

verdict.reasoning:
Concreteness check:
- Trigger: "New file dropped into a shared due-diligence folder (Google Drive)" — this is specific and directly maps to a real Make.com trigger module (Google Drive "Watch Files in a Folder").
- Tools: Google Drive, a document parser (LlamaParse named specifically, though it's really an n8n-side tool — HTTP module equivalent needed), OpenAI for synthesis, output to PDF/Doc. All named concretely.
- Action: parse -> extract figures/risk flags -> compile into structured memo. This is a specific, describable pipeline, not a vague "help with fundraising" category.
So on concreteness, this passes: specific trigger, specific tool names, specific multi-step action chain.

Feasibility check (this is where real scrutiny is needed):
1. Google Drive trigger "watch files in folder" — genuinely a first-class Make.com module. Fine.
2. Document parsing — LlamaParse doesn't have a native Make.com app/module. It would have to be wired via Make's generic HTTP module hitting LlamaParse's REST API (upload doc, poll for job completion, retrieve parsed markdown). That's asynchronous (upload -> poll until ready -> fetch result), which in a no-code workshop is a materially harder pattern than a single request-response call — it typically needs a sleep/repeat-until loop in Make, which is a non-trivial building block for a workshop audience but IS a documented, replicable Make.com pattern (HTTP module + "Repeat until" or a Sleep + iteration). So doable but adds real complexity beyond "connect module A to module B."
3. Multiple file types (financial spreadsheets, legal PDFs, contracts) — realistic DD data rooms contain xlsx, scanned PDFs, docx, sometimes images of signed contracts. A single parser call won't cleanly handle "extract key figures" from an Excel cap table the same way it handles legal risk clauses from a contract PDF. That's a real complexity/feasibility gap: the proposal says "document parser (e.g. LlamaParse)" as if one tool handles this uniformly, but heterogeneous DD documents (cap tables, SAFEs, MSAs, financials) genuinely need different extraction logic per type to produce meaningful "risk flags" — this is understated complexity, though a workshop could simplify to "PDF documents only" and still get a working demo.
4. OpenAI synthesis step — straightforward Make.com OpenAI module (chat completion) taking parsed text and producing structured JSON/markdown summary. This part is genuinely easy and well-trodden.
5. Output to PDF/Doc — Make.com has a Google Docs "Create a Document from Template" module or a PDF-generation module (e.g., via a third-party PDF generator app, or Google Docs API + export as PDF). This is a known, working pattern in existing Make.com templates (proposal-generator, invoice-generator templates all do this). Fine.
6. Source is an n8n workflow being adapted to Make.com, not a native Make.com template — the feasibility label itself says "Medium" and acknowledges it's "more assembly-heavy," which is an honest, appropriately hedged self-assessment rather than an overclaim. That intellectual honesty is a good sign this was evaluated carefully rather than hand-waved.

Net judgment: This is concrete (specific trigger, named tools, named action pipeline, a real source workflow to crib from) and it is feasible on Make.com in simplified form for a workshop — Drive trigger, HTTP-to-parser, OpenAI summarization, Doc/PDF output are all real, wireable Make.com modules. The two soft spots (async polling for the parser step, and heterogeneous DD file types needing more nuanced extraction than one-size-fits-all) mean it's more assembly-heavy than a beginner CRM-notification workflow, which the submission itself flags honestly via the "Medium" feasibility rating. For a workshop, this can be simplified (e.g., restrict to PDF-only uploads, skip polling by using a synchronous parse call or Make's built-in PDF text extraction instead of LlamaParse) to make it buildable in a session, while still preserving the "multi-tool pipeline triggered by a file drop" agentic shape that justifies calling it agentic rather than a single prompt.

This is not a vague, hand-wavy idea — it names an exact trigger, exact tools, and traces to a real reference implementation. It clears the bar for concrete + feasible, with the caveat that the parser step's async/multi-filetype complexity should be simplified for the workshop (e.g., limit to text-based PDFs, skip true job-polling by using a single-call parsing/OCR API) rather than presented as a one-module drag-and-drop.
